unsure.name: I'm not sure
unsure.support: Look at your credit-card or bank statement for a charge from a web hosting company, or search your email for 'hosting' or 'cPanel' - that's who to contact.
php: Find out who hosts your website (see tip below).
Contact them and paste the ready-made message from PatchPulse.
Once they confirm, click 'Check now' in PatchPulse.
files: Ask whoever built or hosts your website to remove the file listed above.
Click 'Check now' afterward to confirm it's gone.

hostinger.name: Hostinger
hostinger.support: Live chat: log in to hPanel and use the Help / chat button.
php: Log in to hPanel at hpanel.hostinger.com.
Open Websites, then click Dashboard (or Manage) next to your site.
Look for 'PHP Configuration' (usually under Advanced) and choose PHP 8.4 or newer.
Hostinger manages the exact security patch level, so also send them the ready-made message to confirm the fix is installed.
files: In hPanel open your website, then 'File Manager'.
Open the public_html folder, find the file listed above, right-click it and Delete.

godaddy.name: GoDaddy
godaddy.support: Phone or chat from your GoDaddy account's Help page.
php: Sign in to GoDaddy, go to My Products, and open cPanel Admin for your hosting.
In cPanel find 'Select PHP Version' or 'MultiPHP Manager'.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer for your site and save.
Send GoDaddy the ready-made message to confirm the security patch is installed.
files: Open cPanel, then 'File Manager'.
Open public_html, select the file listed above, and click Delete.

bluehost.name: Bluehost
bluehost.support: Chat or phone from the Help section of your Bluehost account.
php: Log in to your Bluehost account.
Open your website's settings or the Advanced (cPanel) area and look for 'PHP Version' or 'MultiPHP Manager'.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer and save.
Send Bluehost the ready-made message to confirm the security patch is installed.
files: Open the Advanced (cPanel) area, then 'File Manager'.
Open public_html, select the file listed above, and Delete it.

siteground.name: SiteGround
siteground.support: Open a ticket or chat from the Help Center in your SiteGround account.
php: Log in and open Site Tools for your website.
Go to Devs > PHP Manager.
Pick PHP 8.4 or newer (or the 'Managed PHP' option, which SiteGround keeps updated).
Send SiteGround the ready-made message to confirm the security patch is installed.
files: In Site Tools go to Site > File Manager.
Open public_html, select the file listed above, and Delete it.

namecheap.name: Namecheap
namecheap.support: Live chat from the Namecheap Help Center.
php: Log in to cPanel for your hosting.
Open 'Select PHP Version' (sometimes called 'PHP Selector').
Choose 8.4 or newer and click 'Set as current'.
Send Namecheap the ready-made message to confirm the security patch is installed.
files: Open cPanel > File Manager > public_html.
Select the file listed above and Delete it.

hostgator.name: HostGator
hostgator.support: Chat or phone from your HostGator customer portal.
php: Log in to cPanel.
Open 'MultiPHP Manager' or 'Select PHP Version'.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer for your domain and apply.
Send HostGator the ready-made message to confirm the security patch is installed.
files: Open cPanel > File Manager > public_html.
Select the file listed above and Delete it.

dreamhost.name: DreamHost
dreamhost.support: Contact Support from the DreamHost panel.
php: Log in to the DreamHost panel and open Websites.
Open your site's settings and find the PHP version option.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer and save.
Send DreamHost the ready-made message to confirm the security patch is installed.
files: Use the panel's File Manager (or FTP) to open your site's folder.
Delete the file listed above.

ionos.name: IONOS
ionos.support: Phone or chat from the IONOS Help Center.
php: Log in and open Hosting for your contract.
Find 'PHP version' in your site's settings.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer and save.
Send IONOS the ready-made message to confirm the security patch is installed.
files: Open Webspace Explorer (file manager).
Delete the file listed above.

cpanel.name: Other host with cPanel
cpanel.support: Use your host's support chat or ticket system.
php: Log in to cPanel (often yoursite.com/cpanel).
Open 'MultiPHP Manager' or 'Select PHP Version'.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer and save.
Ask your host to confirm the security patch is installed (ready-made message below).
files: Open cPanel > File Manager > public_html.
Select the file listed above and Delete it.

plesk.name: Host with Plesk
plesk.support: Use your host's support chat or ticket system.
php: Log in to Plesk and open Websites & Domains.
Click 'PHP' (or 'PHP Settings') for your domain.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer and click OK.
Ask your host to confirm the security patch is installed (ready-made message below).
files: In Plesk open Files (File Manager), then httpdocs.
Select the file listed above and Remove it.

managedwp.name: Managed WordPress (WP Engine, Kinsta, Flywheel, etc.)
managedwp.support: Use the support chat in your managed WordPress dashboard - they handle PHP for you.
php: Managed WordPress hosts update PHP for you, but you choose the version.
In your hosting dashboard open your site's settings and look for 'PHP version'.
Choose PHP 8.4 or newer if available.
Send support the ready-made message to confirm the fix is in place.
files: Use your host's file manager or SFTP to delete the file, or ask support to remove it.

vps.name: My own server / VPS
vps.support: You (or your developer) manage this server.
php: Connect to your server with SSH.
Ubuntu/Debian: run   sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade 'php*'   (RHEL/Alma/Rocky: sudo dnf upgrade 'php*').
Restart PHP:   sudo systemctl restart 'php*-fpm' apache2 nginx 2>/dev/null
Check:   php -v   - and click 'Check now' in PatchPulse. Distros often patch without changing the version number; check the package changelog for the CVE numbers.
files: Connect with SSH and delete the file, for example:   sudo rm /var/www/html/.env   (use your real path).
Better: block hidden files in your web server config (nginx: location ~ /\. { deny all; }).

php_upgrade.title: How to update PHP
php_upgrade.intro: PHP is the engine underneath most websites (including every WordPress site). Updating it is usually a setting in your hosting account - you don't need to touch your website's design or content.
php_upgrade.safety: Before changing the PHP version: make a backup (most hosts have a one-click backup). After changing, open your website and click around. If something looks broken, switch back and ask your host or developer for help.

check_file.title: Get your exact PHP version (2 minutes)
check_file.intro: Many hosts hide the PHP version, which is good - but then PatchPulse can't tell whether you're protected. This small file lets PatchPulse (and only PatchPulse) see it.
steps: Click 'Download my check file' below. It contains a secret key made just for this website.
Open your hosting File Manager and go into the main website folder (usually 'public_html', 'www' or 'httpdocs' - the one with index.php in it).
Upload the file there. Keep its name exactly: patchpulse-check.php
Come back here and click 'Check now'. You should see your exact PHP version.
check_file.safety: The file only answers when it receives your secret key, only shares the PHP version and two settings, and never changes anything. Delete it any time.

ssl.title: Fixing the padlock (SSL / https)
ssl.intro: The padlock means visitors' information is encrypted. Almost every host now offers it free (often called 'Let's Encrypt', 'AutoSSL' or 'Free SSL').

exposed_file.title: Removing a file that shouldn't be public
exposed_file.intro: Some files are meant to stay private but were left inside the public website folder. Deleting the file stops the leak - but if it held passwords, change those passwords too, because robots scan for these files constantly.

wordpress.title: Updating WordPress safely
wordpress.intro: WordPress updates fix security holes. Update WordPress itself, then plugins, then themes.
steps: Make a backup first (your host or a backup plugin).
Log in to your WordPress Dashboard (yoursite.com/wp-admin).
Click 'Updates' in the left menu.
Click 'Update to version ...', then update plugins and themes on the same page.
Visit your site to check everything looks right, then click 'Check now' in PatchPulse.

headers.title: Extra browser protection (low priority)
headers.intro: These are optional settings that make browsers add extra protection. Fix red and orange items first. For WordPress, many security plugins add these with one switch.

down.title: When your website is down
down.intro: Check your site from your phone using mobile data (not Wi-Fi). If it's down there too, contact your host. If you recently updated a plugin or theme, mention that - it's the most common cause.

wp_plugin.title: Updating a WordPress plugin
wp_plugin.intro: Plugins add features to WordPress, and out-of-date plugins are the most common way WordPress sites get broken into.
steps: Make a backup first (your host or a backup plugin).
Log in to your WordPress Dashboard (yoursite.com/wp-admin).
Click 'Plugins' in the left menu.
Find the plugin named in this message and click 'Update now'. If there's no update button, deactivate and delete the plugin until a fixed version is released.
Visit your site to check everything still works, then click 'Check now' in PatchPulse.

server.title: Updating the web server software
server.intro: The web server (Apache or nginx) is the program that delivers your website to visitors. On regular hosting your hosting company updates it, so the ready-made message is usually all you need.

cms.title: Updating your site builder
cms.intro: Drupal and Joomla release security updates regularly. Your web developer or host can apply them; make a backup first.

integrity.title: When something on your site changed
integrity.intro: PatchPulse remembers what outside code your homepage loads. When something new shows up, check whether you or your developer added it. If nobody did, treat it as urgent: change your website and hosting passwords and contact your host.

protect.title: Keep this website protected
protect.intro: These are the protections you can switch on yourself, once, so many future fixes happen without you. PatchPulse opens the right screen; you click the switch. Tick each one off when it's done.

items.title: Turn on automatic WordPress updates
steps: Click 'Open WordPress updates' below and log in.
Near the top of the page, click 'Enable automatic updates for all new versions of WordPress' (if it says they're already on, you're done).
Keep a backup running: most hosts include one, or use a backup plugin.

items.title: Turn on automatic plugin updates
steps: Click 'Open WordPress plugins' below and log in.
In the 'Automatic Updates' column, click 'Enable auto-updates' next to each plugin you trust.
Delete plugins you no longer use: they can still be broken into even when switched off.

items.title: Choose a supported PHP version and turn on automatic security updates if your host offers it
steps: Open your hosting control panel.
Find the PHP version setting (steps for your host are in the PHP fix guide) and choose 8.4 or newer.
If your host offers 'managed' or 'automatic' PHP updates, turn that on.

items.title: Turn on the website firewall your host or CDN already provides
steps: Open your hosting control panel and look for a 'Security' section. Many hosts include a website firewall or malware scanner you can switch on.
If your site uses Cloudflare: log in at dash.cloudflare.com, open your website, then Security, and make sure the managed security rules are switched on.
If you're not sure whether you have one, send your host the message below.
items.support_ask: Does my hosting plan include a website firewall (WAF) or malware protection, and can you make sure it's switched on for my site?

items.title: Make sure automatic backups are on
steps: Open your hosting control panel and look for 'Backups'.
Check that daily automatic backups are switched on, and note how to restore one.
A recent backup makes every update safe to try.
items.support_ask: Are daily automatic backups switched on for my website, and how do I restore one?
